The banana you eat
today is not the
banana your grandparents ate.
The world has already
lived through one banana
crisis, and another may
be starting right now.
For much of the
first half of the
twentieth century, the
banana trade was dominated
by a variety called
the Gros Michel,
nicknamed Big Mike.
It had a thick
skin and grew in
heavy bunches that could
be shipped whole,
on the stem,
without bruising easily.
Many people described its
flavor as richer and
sweeter than the Cavendish.
Like every commercial
banana, the Gros Michel
was grown from cuttings,
so whole plantations were
clones.
In a varied crop,
some plants carry natural
differences that help them
survive.
In a field of
clones, if a disease
can kill one plant,
it can kill them all.
Starting in the late
1800s, a soil fungus
called Fusarium oxysporum,
in a form known
as Tropical Race 1,
spread through banana
plantations in Central
America.
It entered through the
roots and clogged the
plant's water-carrying
tissues.
The disease became known
as Panama disease.
Its spores can survive
in the soil for
decades, and no fungicide
could clear the infected
fields.
By the middle of
the twentieth century,
large areas of infected
land were abandoned.
The rescue was a
variety called the
Cavendish, named for William
Cavendish, the sixth Duke
of Devonshire, whose
Chatsworth greenhouse grew
early plants that had
come by way of Mauritius.
The Cavendish could resist
Tropical Race 1.
Many described the Cavendish
as less flavorful and
more delicate, but it
resisted the disease and
gave good harvests,
so the world switched to it.
Today, nearly all the
bananas exported to wealthy
countries are Cavendish,
with estimates ranging
from about ninety-five
to ninety-nine percent.
Then a newer strain
of the fungus,
called Tropical Race 4,
appeared.
It can attack the Cavendish.
It was confirmed in
Colombia in 2019,
in Peru in 2021,
and in Venezuela in 2023.
Once it is in
a field, its spores
can stay in the
soil for decades.
Researchers are fighting
back with a genetically
modified Cavendish called
QCAV-4, approved in
Australia in 2024,
as well as gene
editing and breeding.
Many experts also say
we need more variety.
